candidate.blueprint_locator: Management of Care client-needs subcategory (15–21% of items), within Safe and Effective Care Environment; this item tests coordinated client education, follow-up planning, and escalation of care.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Client education and escalation planning for asthma control and attacks
candidate.educational_objective: Use a provider-developed written asthma action plan to guide individualized daily control, early response to worsening symptoms, and timely escalation for urgent or emergency care.

options.A: To give the client individualized instructions for routine control, worsening symptoms, and when urgent medical care is needed
options.B: To replace ongoing follow-up with the health care provider once asthma is stable
options.C: To delay use of prescribed reliever treatment until symptoms become severe
options.D: To use the same treatment steps for every person with asthma regardless of symptoms or provider instructions

candidate.rationale: A is correct. Current CDC guidance states that everyone with asthma needs an individual Asthma Action Plan created with a health care provider. The plan organizes actions according to asthma status, including what to do when doing well, when asthma is getting worse, and when there is a medical alert. Current NHLBI guidance likewise describes a written action plan as a provider-developed treatment plan that tells the client how to monitor and treat symptoms, which medicines to take and when, and when to call the provider or seek emergency care. B, C, and D contradict individualized asthma self-management and escalation planning.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Current federal guidance directly supports individualized written asthma action plans that translate current control or worsening symptoms into predefined treatment and escalation actions.
candidate.source_document_title: Living with Asthma; Asthma - Treatment and Action Plan
candidate.source_locator: CDC 'Living with Asthma' → 'Asthma Action Plans': everyone with asthma needs their own plan created with a health care provider; Green Zone, Yellow Zone, and Red Zone sections give actions for doing well, worsening asthma, and medical alert. NHLBI 'Asthma - Treatment and Action Plan' → 'Create an asthma action plan': the written treatment plan identifies triggers, how to recognize an attack and what to do, medicines and timing, when to call the provider or go to the emergency room, and emergency contacts.
candidate.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), corroborated by National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI/NIH)
